sections.skill: Evaluate how education, skills, and the labor market affect lifetime income

questions.prompt: Which is an example of investing in your "human capital"?
questions.intro: Human capital is the knowledge, skills, and experience that make a person productive and able to earn income. Education, training, apprenticeships, and work experience build human capital, often raising future earnings.
questions.feedback: An apprenticeship builds skills that raise earning power: human capital.
sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Employment Projections): Median weekly earnings rise and unemployment rates fall with higher educational attainment (figures update yearly). (https://www.bls.gov/emp/chart-unemployment-earnings-education.htm)

questions.prompt: Pat can work now at $32,000 per year, or attend a 4-year program first. What is the opportunity cost in earnings of the 4 years in school (ignoring raises)?
questions.intro: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best choice you give up. The cost of school includes tuition and also the income you could have earned while studying.
sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Employment Projections): Median weekly earnings rise and unemployment rates fall with higher educational attainment (figures update yearly). (https://www.bls.gov/emp/chart-unemployment-earnings-education.htm)

questions.prompt: Path A: start work at 18 earning $32,000 a year. Path B: start at 22 earning $52,000 a year. Ignoring raises and costs, which path has earned more by age 40, and by how much?
questions.intro: Comparing career paths over many years shows the trade-off: a later start can be outweighed by higher yearly earnings, depending on the numbers and costs.
sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Employment Projections): Median weekly earnings rise and unemployment rates fall with higher educational attainment (figures update yearly). (https://www.bls.gov/emp/chart-unemployment-earnings-education.htm)

questions.prompt: Demand for wind turbine technicians rises sharply, but few people have the training. What usually happens to their wages?
questions.intro: Wages are influenced by supply and demand in the labor market. When employers need more workers with a skill than are available, wages for that skill tend to rise. When many people have a skill employers need less, wages tend to fall.
questions.feedback: High demand and limited supply of a skill push wages up (12-5a).

misconceptions.B: Thinks wages are set by law

sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Employment Projections): Median weekly earnings rise and unemployment rates fall with higher educational attainment (figures update yearly). (https://www.bls.gov/emp/chart-unemployment-earnings-education.htm)

questions.prompt: Software that automates routine bookkeeping becomes common. Which outcome is MOST likely?

choices.text: All accounting jobs disappear within a single year
No effect on jobs, because technology never changes work
Higher pay for every routine data-entry job
Fewer routine jobs, more need for analysis skills

questions.correct_answer: Fewer routine jobs, more need for analysis skills
questions.feedback: Technology often replaces routine tasks and raises demand for workers who can use the tools and do analysis (12-5b).

sections.relationship: Comparing career and education choices depends on recognizing what is given up.

questions.prompt: Lia can work a Saturday shift for $120 or go to a free concert. If she goes to the concert, what is the opportunity cost?

choices.text: The price of a ticket she did not buy

questions.intro: Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the next-best option you give up. A "free" activity can still cost the money or time you could have used otherwise.
questions.feedback: She gives up $120 of pay, the next-best option.

misconceptions.D: Confuses the choice with what is given up

questions.prompt: Which is the opportunity cost of spending $50 on a video game?

choices.text: What else the $50 could have done
The time it takes to drive to the store
The sales tax on the game

questions.correct_answer: What else the $50 could have done
questions.feedback: Money spent one way cannot be used for the next-best alternative.

misconceptions.B: Part of cost but not the main idea here
misconceptions.C: Confuses opportunity cost with an added cost

questions.prompt: Why do many careers that require more training pay more?

choices.text: The law requires higher pay for degrees
Training programs set the wages their graduates earn
The skills are scarce and valued

questions.correct_answer: The skills are scarce and valued
questions.intro: Specialized skills take time and money to gain, so fewer people have them. When employers need those skills, they compete for workers by offering higher pay.
questions.feedback: Scarce, valuable skills tend to earn higher wages.

sections.skill: When does more education pay off?

questions.prompt: Path A earns $32,000 a year starting now. Path B costs $40,000 for a 4-year program, then earns $52,000 a year. Let t = years from now (t ≥ 4). Which equation finds when their total earnings (B net of the program cost) are equal?
questions.intro: A "break-even point" is when two options have produced the same total. Write each option's total as an expression in t (years), set them equal, and solve.
questions.feedback: Path A has earned 32,000t. Path B has earned 52,000(t − 4) after its 4 school years, minus its $40,000 cost.

misconceptions.B: Forgets that Path B earns nothing for 4 years
misconceptions.C: Puts the delay on the wrong path
misconceptions.D: Adds the cost to Path A and ignores the delay

questions.prompt: Military service, community college, and certifications are all ways to build skills. What do they have in common financially?

Each guarantees a high salary right after finishing

questions.prompt: Data show workers with more education tend to have lower unemployment rates. How should a student use this fact?

choices.text: As proof that any degree guarantees a job in any field
As a reason to ignore program costs
As a reason to avoid all training
As one input among costs, interests, and demand

questions.correct_answer: As one input among costs, interests, and demand
questions.feedback: Averages describe groups, not guarantees; costs and field demand also matter.

misconceptions.A: Treats an average as a guarantee
